#6077. The Billion-Dollar Companies Behind Half Of The World's Commercial Aircraft

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

While household names such as United Airlines and Lufthansa dominate the skies in terms of fleet count, there are many companies in existence that have similarly sized fleets that do not carry passengers or cargo, nor do they operate charter missions. These companies never sell a ticket, operate a route, or pursue significant branding campaigns.

Some of these firms control fleets worth tens of billions of dollars, and one owns more aircraft than many of the airlines the public recognizes. The airline industry is composed primarily of two main financial systems: ownership and lease.

Many companies such as Delta Air Lines are known for owning a high percentage of their fleet, notably their older Boeing 717 or Boeing 767 fleets. However, the majority of airlines lease a portion of their jets, as many aircraft with long order backlogs at the manufacturer itself can be hard to obtain. Leasing is a common way to bypass delivery delays.

Most people assume airlines buy the aircraft they fly. Increasingly, that is not the case. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), leasing now accounts for more than half of the world's commercial fleet, making aircraft leasing one of the most important yet least visible sectors in aviation.

Rather than purchasing aircraft outright, many airlines rent them under long-term agreements from specialized leasing companies. The scale of those firms is difficult to appreciate until their fleets are examined. AerCap, the world's largest aircraft lessor, reported owning 1,501 aircraft and managing another 148 at the end of 2025, with an additional 283 aircraft on order.

Those figures make AerCap a larger aircraft owner than many of the world's biggest airlines. Meanwhile, competitors such as SMBC Aviation Capital, Avolon, BOC Aviation, and Air Lease Corporation collectively control thousands more aircraft worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

However, ownership and operation are not the same thing. If airlines do not own many of the aircraft they fly, why would they willingly hand that responsibility to someone else? While there are many sides to the discussion, the answer relates to the complexities of operating an airplane to begin with, which is far more involved than car or boat ownership, for example.

A new Boeing 787-9 carries a list price exceeding $300 million, while even narrowbody aircraft represent investments worth tens of millions of dollars each. Purchasing hundreds of aircraft outright would require enormous amounts of capital that airlines often prefer to dedicate elsewhere. Dry leasing is the most common and most cost-effective way to accomplish this cost benefit.

Aircraft leasing allows airlines to expand fleets without making the full upfront purchase themselves. Instead, leasing firms acquire aircraft from manufacturers such as Boeing and Airbus and lease them to airlines over periods that frequently range from six to twelve years. Airlines gain access to modern aircraft while preserving cash and reducing financial risk.

Hundreds of owned and investor-serviced aircraft

Hundreds of owned aircraft and major order book

While having direct operating authority of 1,066 aircraft, United Airlines' fleet also includes a subsection of leased aircraft, according to the SEC. This figure comprises 958 owned and 108 leased, at the end of 2025. This number is significantly less than AerCap's total number of active leases, which, on paper, causes AerCap to resemble a major international airline.

Four leasing companies own thousands of the aircraft that airlines fly every day. Here is how large their fleets are and how they got there.

In practice, passengers rarely notice that a different company owns the aircraft they are flying on. Under a dry lease, the lessor provides the aircraft while the airline supplies its own pilots, maintenance program, insurance, and operating certificates. To passengers, the aircraft appears no different from any other jet in the airline's fleet.

One recent example comes from Avolon's reported October 2025 sale-and-leaseback agreement with TAAG Angola Airlines involving 787-9 aircraft. In that arrangement, the aircraft are operated by TAAG, but ownership remains with the leasing company. Similar transactions occur throughout the industry and frequently involve new aircraft deliveries from Boeing and Airbus. An aircraft may spend its entire operational life flying for airlines that never technically own it.

A wet lease is an entirely different form of leasing, provided by companies like Heston Airlines, Hi Fly, or Wamos Air. The aircraft is frequently in the livery of the lessor, although not always. Further, the in-flight service, cabin crew, and standards are all those of the lessor company. Wet leases generally have a higher cost than dry leases, and are generally shorter in term.

The influence of lessors extends far beyond simple ownership. Because companies such as AerCap, Avolon, and SMBC Aviation Capital place enormous aircraft orders, they have become some of Boeing's and Airbus' most important customers. Lessors routinely order aircraft years before identifying the airlines that will eventually operate them.

This purchasing power became especially significant during recent supply chain constraints. CAPA reports that aircraft shortages and production delays have strengthened lessors' market positions by increasing aircraft values and lease rates. Airlines seeking growth often cannot wait years for new direct deliveries, making leased aircraft one of the few available solutions.

The result is that lessors frequently influence what aircraft manufacturers build, how quickly airlines can expand, and even which carriers gain access to modern fleets. A major leasing company may place an order measured in hundreds of aircraft, a scale that rivals the purchasing power of many national airlines.

Orders placed by airlines themselves to manufacturers such as Boeing or Airbus are typically more noteworthy. They represent a larger upfront financial commitment and a known destination for production aircraft. Orders placed by lessors are less noteworthy, but still significant from an operational standpoint.

While the end user of the aircraft is not known when, for example, AerCap placed an order for 100 Airbus jets, such an order boosts the inventory of a lessor. This not only provides options for customers, but an entirely different, and at times, more accessible way of expanding a fleet.

Leasing an aircraft engine is expensive, especially in today's industry.

The growing importance of lessors is increasingly tied to aircraft scarcity. Airbus and Boeing continue to work through substantial backlogs measured in thousands of aircraft. For airlines needing capacity sooner rather than later, leasing companies often represent the fastest available path to fleet growth.

Leasing companies also offer smaller airlines and startup carriers alike a lower barrier to entry to operation than buying an aircraft outright from the producer. AerCap provides one of the clearest examples. The company website published an order book of 283 aircraft entering 2026 while simultaneously managing thousands of aviation assets, including engines and helicopters.

That position effectively allows it to act as a bridge between manufacturers producing aircraft and airlines seeking them. Manufacturers in the aviation industry have the greatest amount of market control for their product. However, some of that power can be relinquished when a customer also acts as a distributor. The relationship between the manufacturer and the lessor creates an unusual balance of power.

Manufacturers remain responsible for designing and producing aircraft, but the largest lessors have amassed order books so large that they have become some of Airbus' and Boeing's most important customers. Companies such as AerCap regularly place orders measured in the hundreds of aircraft, allowing them to negotiate from a position of strength while shaping fleet decisions across dozens of airlines simultaneously.

The future significance of aircraft lessors will likely depend on one simple metric: access to aircraft. Airlines can only grow as quickly as new aircraft become available, and both Airbus and Boeing continue to hold order backlogs extending years into the future. Major aircraft manufacturers, while experiencing high backlogs of orders and record customer interest, can lose control of the end use of their product when lessors place massive orders.

That reality places unusual attention on companies such as AerCap, Avolon, and SMBC Aviation Capital. Their order books, delivery positions, and financing capabilities may determine which airlines can launch new routes, replace aging fleets, or enter emerging markets first.

In an industry built around aircraft availability, the companies holding the keys to future deliveries may become as important as the carriers operating them. The next major test will come as manufacturers work through production constraints and thousands of aircraft currently sitting in order backlogs move toward delivery.

Whether airlines continue shifting toward leased fleets or return to greater ownership could depend on how effectively Boeing and Airbus satisfy demand over the remainder of the decade. For passengers, the aircraft parked at the gate will probably continue wearing airline colors. The more interesting question is whether the real power behind those fleets increasingly belongs to companies whose names never appear on the boarding pass.

#6076. On Location: Dig Stars Amy Poehler and Geraldine Viswanathan on Italian Gelato, Go-Karting—and Tailgating

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Dig.

Amy Poehler had never been to Greece, but she was immediately entranced by Kate Myers’s novel Excavations about four women coming together for an archaeological dig in Athens. So she took her first trip there to set the scene for her 10-part Peacock comedy series Dig, which drops November 23.

“The way in which Greek people mingle with real antiquities every day, walking past very important structures, is archaeology in process,” the Saturday Night Live alum tells Traveler. “The old and the new are constantly bumping up against each other. It was very cool to be there and really helped remind us of the theme of the show that the past is just around the corner and you can't hide from it.”

Each of the characters comes to the dig site at different stage of their life, with Poehler as an archaeologist stuck as second fiddle to beloved Neville (Hugh Laurie). But it’s her bond with fellow diggers, heartbroken free spirit Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), young and flustered Patty (Fina Strazza), and refined but ready to rebel Clare (Antonia Thomas) that provides the backbone of the series—a coming of age story for every age.

Despite being set purely in Greece, Poehler says they quickly found that “Puglia wine country, Greece, and Los Angeles can kind of double for each other, which is weird." So the team made southeastern Italy their home base, checking in at Rocco Forte's Masseria Torre Maizza, where they indulged in seafood (“We got overwhelmed by how good the food was!”) and bought tons of pottery wherever they traveled, a side effect of talking about it on the show so much.

Off-set, they found high-speed fun, thanks to the keen ears of Laurie. “We could hear the roar of go-karts from our hotel, so he went around on a motorbike—he's so cool—and found this place,” Viswanathan says of Circuit Kart Evolution in Fasano. Poehler jumps in: “The crew and most of the cast raced, but a couple of outsider Europeans who snuck in ended up winning because they had the real lead foot!”

Amy Poehler's 10-part Peacock series films all across the Mediterranean.

As for where a second season could take them, the cast will only drop hints. Viswanathan says it will be “a little spicier," while Poehler adds “it would be more passionate and fiery." But one thing's for sure, they are ready to start digging again soon. "We have some ideas for where to go and what kind of stuff we could dig up,” Poehler says. “Archeological digs are in a lot of different countries, so we could go all over!”

With her executive producer hat on, Poehler really honed in on the details of Greek culture during her time in Athens, in order to capture that same essence on screen. “I’m a New Yorker, so Athens is a really cool, vibrant, interesting city, but it does have a lot more graffiti than we expected,” she admits, adding that “some of it is really beautiful.” That meant they had to add that grittiness to some of their recreated sets in Italy and California. Another unique aspect: “the light in Greece is so specific and beautiful,” she says of the natural rays. The best part? “We got to wrap and then go have the best salad you’d ever had in your life—I’m still thinking about it.” Her favorite was a meal at Barbounaki, where “the guy basically said trust me and came back with a whole fish and cut it at the table—it was so good.”

The fifth-century BCE Temple of Poseidon serves as an epic ancient backdrop in Dig.

Just over an hour’s drive southeast of Athens stands the remains of the Doric-style Temple of Poseidon, dating back to the mid-fifth century BCE, where Poehler and Laurie filmed. “Talk about set decoration—you’re standing in front of something so amazing,” she says of the ruins at the end of Cape Sounion overlooking the Aegean Sea. The sacred place is even mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey, so needless to say, it’s also a busy tourist attraction. “We had to get there at the crack of dawn before the tours,” Poehler says, noting that the landmark’s staff was standing behind them counting down the minutes they had left. “That’s tough when you’re doing an emotional scene and you know someone wants to get you out of there.” But eventually they did have to open to the public as the cameras kept rolling. “It was funny to be pretending to have this conversation when there’s an American tourist behind you in the shot eating a bag of jelly beans.”

The port town of Monopoli provided the rich seaside vibe to double as Greece. Viswanathan says the initial montage where viewers are introduced to her character Dylan when she wakes up on a bench and asks for directions to the dig site was all in town, “which was so dreamy.” Poehler particularly loved the shopping scenes in its old town, including one with Laurie, shot at the hat shop Castrignano dal 1923 (sharp-eyed viewers will see it retains its Italian signage despite being set in Greece). “We wanted a place that Neville would go to pick out his hat for the year, and of course because it’s Italy, there was a beautiful old hat store in the middle of Monopoli and we used some of their hats.”

At Polignano a Mare, Poehler and co-creator Michael Schur kept open a local gelato stand for the public to enjoy free scoops.

Known for its dramatic scenery and crescent beaches, Polignano a Mare is best remembered to the duo for its most famous treat. “Gelato, so much gelato—Amy let the whole town eat gelato,” Viswanathan revealed. Indeed, after filming at a stand in town, Poehler and co-creator Michael Schur kept it open for the public to enjoy free scoops too. “Then Mike reminded me that I have not paid my half,” she admits. Despite being lactose intolerant, Viswanathan has a sweet spot for hazelnut, while Poehler is all about stracciatella, a refined form of chocolate chip. “I have to say, as an American, chocolate chip is very hard to find—it’s being replaced by mint chip,” to which her co-star replies, “ That’s so not right.”

The crew also headed inland to the hilltop town of Carovigno with a medieval fortress and a compact city center, which provided the bones for their set. “The locals were very interested in the fact that a production came in and shut down their town square and changed all of the store signs to Greek,” Poehler says. Viswanathan adds: “They were like, these Americans are confused—and lost!” But to get there, they also had to navigate the distinctly Italian way of driving. “It was intense—they come up really close and tailgate in a real way,” Poehler said. “You’ve got to get out of the way!”

Some of the Mediterranean scenery was recreated on a Universal Studios backlot in California.

Back on the Universal Studios backlot, set designer Dan Bishop—who’s worked on Mad Men and Parks and Recreation—recreated the Greek settings and dig site. “He and his team went over to Greece and got a bunch of local beer and signs, so when we were shooting in Los Angeles, it was really fun to be around all the stuff that felt authentic, from the colors and flowers to the buildings—it’s really important to get a feel of that.” But there was one twist that was distinctly Hollywood. “At times we could hear the Fast and Furious: [Hollywood Drift] roller coaster while we were shooting,” Poehler said of the theme park ride that opened in September, after they filmed. “We were hearing them do test runs—it’s open now, which is really exciting,” Viswanathan says. While she hadn't been on it yet, she commented, “the night is young.” As for Poehler, she's most happy with her feet firmly on the ground.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6075. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6074. Air New Zealand Denied All Slots For New 27-Hour Route: Here's Why

Air New Zealand has been looking to return to the UK market for some time. The last time we saw its black-and-white livery was in March 2020, when it operated its final flight from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) to Auckland International Airport (AKL). Since then, passengers traveling between the UK and New Zealand have had to rely on connecting flights through hubs in the Middle East, Asia or Australia.

That being said, for the upcoming summer 2027 season, the New Zealand flag carrier had sought to secure slots at Heathrow. According to Airport Coordination Limited's (ACL) Initial Coordination Report for London Heathrow, the Star Alliance member requested 434 slots for the season. However, none of these were approved.

Air New Zealand had been flying to London for several decades. The airline initially served London Gatwick Airport (LGW) from Auckland, with stops in Papeete, Tahiti, and Los Angeles. In 1994, it moved its operations to Heathrow, where it continued to fly via Los Angeles. Between 2006 and 2013, the airline also offered flights via Hong Kong.

However, the Star Alliance member eventually decided to discontinue its London service due to low passenger numbers. It is unclear what routing it would have used had it secured the slots for summer 2027. Los Angeles appears to have been one possibility, as a spokesperson previously told Simple Flying that the airline would most likely operate the service via the US city using Boeing 777 aircraft.

Interestingly, Air New Zealand had also applied for slots at London Gatwick for the previous summer season and was actually successful in securing them. However, the airline never launched the flights, as it was facing aircraft availability issues at the time. Up to four of its 14 Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners were grounded simultaneously due to problems with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines and maintenance delays.

These aircraft have since returned to service. Nevertheless, aircraft availability remains a concern. According to ch-aviation, Air New Zealand currently has nine 777-300ERs and 16 787-9s, although only 11 of the latter are in active service. The airline is also awaiting deliveries of three additional 787-9s and five 787-10s, with its outstanding Dreamliner orders expected to be fulfilled by 2028.

However, Boeing has faced difficulties increasing 787 production to its target of ten aircraft per month, partly due to supply-chain delays involving General Electric GEnx engines. These issues have affected deliveries to customers, including Air New Zealand, although planespotters.net data shows that the airline received two Dreamliners in October 2026.

Apart from new aircraft deliveries, the Star Alliance member is also refurbishing its existing widebody fleet. As of late October, 13 of its 14 787-9s had completed cabin upgrades, which include replacing the older inward-facing Business Premier seats with private suites, updating Economy cabins and introducing bunk-style sleeping pods on selected aircraft.

The final Dreamliner is expected to return to service before the end of the year. The airline is also scheduled to begin refurbishing its 777 fleet in March 2027. All of which are expected to undergo the upgrades by the end of 2027, meaning aircraft will need to be temporarily withdrawn from service while the work takes place.

Air New Zealand is one of the principal airlines operating in the South Pacific, with a fleet for NZ's domestic needs and ultra-long-haul routes.

The exact reason why Air New Zealand did not receive any slots has not been confirmed. However, Heathrow is one of the most slot-constrained airports in the world, and securing additional slots is difficult. According to ACL's report, airlines requested a total of 26,832 slots for summer 2027, but only 151 were allocated, just 0.6% of the requests.

Xiamen Air, which recently launched a weekly service between Xiamen and Heathrow, received most of the approved slots. However, several other airlines were unsuccessful. These included Alaska Airlines, which only began flying to Heathrow from Seattle in May and requested 434 slots for next summer. Emirates also failed to secure any of the 1,920 slots it requested, while Virgin Atlantic, Delta Air Lines, Air India and Riyadh Air were denied all 1,798, 556, 1,736 and 868 slots they sought, respectively.

#6072. Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

The airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

The redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

In recent years, first-class, business-class and premium economy have stolen many of the headlines when it comes to air travel — and there’s a big reason for that.

Airlines have leaned heavily into premium seating, with the fancy suites and recliners serving as the biggest money-makers on the plane.

That has led to a ton of luxe new suites and features, like United's Polaris Studios which debuted earlier this year with 27-inch screens.

At the same time, we’re also seeing some intriguing new innovations in economy, too.

To be clear, the seats aren’t suddenly getting wider, and the legroom isn’t magically improving.

But a growing number of airlines are rolling out some new options and upgrades that should ultimately lead to more enjoyable flights, without the need to pay thousands of dollars (or hundreds of thousands of points).

For starters, there’s the Wi-Fi. It has long been a pain point for travelers, as they'd be stuck paying a fee for an often-spotty service.

Nearly all of the large U.S. carriers now offer — or have plans to offer — on-board internet free to members of their loyalty programs.

Most U.S. airlines are installing or preparing to install ultrafast service from Starlink, which is widely regarded as the fastest Wi-Fi in the sky today.

The days of being disconnected when you fly are fast disappearing.

Whenever I sleep on a red-eye flight in coach, I tend to wake up with a sore neck.

This year, Emirates debuted a new feature that should help.

Its "U-Dream" setup has side wings that cradle your neck as you sleep. You can see what it looks like below.

Swipe to see me trying out a "generic" version of the concept at an aviation conference last year.

If you're going to be in economy, that headrest looks like it would definitely make the experience more comfortable — especially on a long flight from the U.S. to Dubai.

Walk-up snack bars are popping up on some commercial planes, which double as a way to stretch your legs during a long flight — and get some sustenance at 35,000 feet.

United used the last row of its new Airbus A321XLR for a snack bar, which will be a nice option for passengers flying that single-aisle plane on long-haul routes.

A handful of additional U.S. carriers have announced plans to offer their snack bars in the sky in the near future. JetBlue has offered a snack "pantry" for years on its long-range planes.

Don’t want to splurge on a pricey business-class or premium economy seat?

United recently announced it would join Air New Zealand in offering a couch, of sorts, in economy.

Next year, the carrier plans to debut a product it’s calling its “Relax Row” on some long-haul flights.

Available as a paid add-on, the concept allows you to turn three economy seats into one "bed." The airline has framed this as a strong option for families traveling together.

The setup is similar to the “Skycouch" Air New Zealand has offered on its long transpacific flights for years.

United plans to outfit some of its largest twin-aisle jets with the “Relax Row,” including some Boeing 777 and 787 aircraft.

How much would you pay for a few hours of shut-eye?

Air New Zealand plans to one-up itself soon with a new bunk-bed in coach.

The new “Skynest” concept will feature two sets of bunk beds stacked three high, with a ladder to reach the upper bunks.

Passengers will be able to book a four-hour nap for an additional fee of $495.

It’s not business-class, but if your only goal is to get some sleep on a long flight from the U.S. to New Zealand, it could be well worth it.

Speaking of ultra-long journeys, Qantas is preparing to launch the world’s longest flights.

Its “Project Sunrise” service from Sydney to London is scheduled to start in October 2027. The service will be followed by flights from Sydney to New York City.

On board the ultra-long-range Airbus A350-1000, passengers won’t just find new premium seating options.

There will also be a “well-being zone,” where passengers can walk around, stretch — and maybe even do a few exercises.

That movement is crucial on flights that will span nearly a full day in the air.

Meanwhile, even as passengers board with multiple screens and devices in their bags, airlines are doubling down on seatback screens.

In the U.S., they’re already a staple on United, Delta Air Lines and JetBlue.

But carriers are also upgrading their seatback entertainment with better headphone technology, streaming services and entertainment options.

United has been working to equip all of its seatback devices with Bluetooth pairing technology, which allows passengers to connect their Apple AirPods and similar devices to the screens.

The carrier also recently rolled out a new partnership with Spotify, which lets flyers stream from their accounts on the seatback screen.

Delta, meanwhile, has launched a seatback partnership with YouTube — and is preparing to deploy new, next-generation screens with a host of new inflight features.

As all of that unfolds, American is pivoting back to screens after removing them from its planes years ago. It will be some time before they are widely available, though.

Airlines have also struck up content partnerships with major newspapers (like the Delta-Wall Street Journal tie-up) and streaming platforms (like United’s with Apple TV+).

We’ve come a long way from the days when the whole plane would watch the same movie on communal screens.

#6070. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6069. JSX Buys Bankrupt Airline In Major Expansion Beyond 30-Seat Semi-Private Flights

JSX has acquired bankrupt New Pacific Airlines, securing a regulatory pathway to operate aircraft with more than 30 passenger seats. The airline, which abandoned its ambitious Boeing 757 operation in November 2025, was acquired in August 2026, although the deal only became public following a November 20 Department of Transportation (DOT) filing, as reported by AeroTime.

Rather than introducing new aircraft, JSX intends to transfer existing Embraer ERJ145-LRs into the acquired airline, increasing seating capacity from 30 to 42 passengers. The acquisition also creates opportunities beyond its immediate plans, potentially including higher-capacity turboprops, while providing greater flexibility amid ongoing regulatory scrutiny of JSX's operating model.

JSX reportedly acquired New Pacific for approximately $3.1 million in consideration. According to the November 20 DOT filing, the airline intends to restart operations under the JSX Air brand using two ERJ145-LRs leased from sister company Delux Public Charter, increasing to six aircraft by the fifth month. Projections include 10,106 flights and approximately 309,000 passenger boardings during the first year.

The key acquisition is New Pacific's FAA Part 121 operating certificate. JSX currently flies under Part 135, selling individual seats through the Part 380 public charter framework. This limits its aircraft to 30 passenger seats, even though its Embraer jets were originally designed to carry more. New Pacific's certificate provides a pathway to operate 42-seat aircraft, subject to regulatory approvals.

The move also offers regulatory flexibility. AP News previously reported how the FAA has proposed tightening oversight of public charter operators, following criticism from major airlines and pilot unions. Although those changes remain unresolved, a Part 121 operation could provide JSX with an alternative growth platform. Responding to questions about the acquisition, the company told View From The Wing:

"JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more customers and more communities. As part of that work, we are pursuing additional pathways that could provide even more ways to deliver our award-winning service in the future."

Originally known as Northern Pacific Airways, the airline planned to connect North America with Japan and South Korea through Anchorage, using Boeing 757-200 aircraft. Inspired by Icelandair's connecting-hub model, the strategy unraveled following Russian airspace restrictions in 2022. The carrier lacked the ETOPS approval required for alternative routings, forcing management to seek other markets.

In July 2023, the airline instead launched domestic flights between Ontario, California, and Las Vegas, subsequently adding Reno and Nashville. Rebranded as New Pacific Airlines in September 2023, it abandoned scheduled operations in April 2024 to focus on charter flights. Management then pursued corporate and sports-team charters, converting its Boeing 757s from 181 seats to just 78 premium seats.

Russian airspace restrictions disrupt plans

Flying ends; approximately 115 employees laid off

However, neither business model proved sustainable. According to January 2026 bankruptcy documents, the wider group burned approximately $5 million monthly during its earlier difficulties, while the NHL contract initially lost money on every flight. Expensive Boeing 757 maintenance and disputed payments worsened liquidity problems. Operations ceased in November last year, and the airline's Part 121 certificate became an important asset in bankruptcy proceedings.

The end of an era for a carrier that experienced more than its fair share of struggles.

JSX's immediate plans involve six 42-seat ERJ145s, where it can increase capacity per aircraft by 40% over the current 30-seat layout. Paxex.aero reports that proposed routes would average 230–345 miles (370–556 km), with approximately six daily sectors per aircraft. Higher capacity could improve economics, although retaining JSX's spacious cabin, currently featuring individual seats and side tables on some aircraft, may become challenging.

The acquisition could also benefit JSX's turboprop strategy. The airline introduced ATR 42-600 flights in December 2025 with 30 premium seats per aircraft, and has outlined plans for up to 25 ATR aircraft, potentially including the larger ATR 72-600. Under Part 121, both types could theoretically accommodate substantially more passengers, provided New Pacific secures the necessary aircraft-specific operating approvals.

Only the 42-seat ERJ145 configuration has been announced. Higher-capacity ATR operations remain hypothetical.

Ultimately, JSX could develop two complementary offerings: its established 30-seat premium service and higher-capacity flights under Part 121. Its expanding ATR operation already demonstrates a willingness to diversify aircraft types, while New Pacific's certificate offers flexibility to accommodate further growth. The acquisition therefore gives JSX more than additional seats: it provides an alternative regulatory platform without requiring the airline to abandon its existing business model.

#6068. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

When you're applying for a credit card, you may wonder: "How good is the welcome offer I'm applying for?"

There's no simple answer to this question, but knowing the previous offers a card has had can help you determine what constitutes a good welcome offer. Getting any welcome offer is better than getting nothing at all, but you wouldn't want to apply for a card only to see a better offer a month later.

Generally, you’ll want good to excellent credit to qualify for many of the Capital One cards on this list, though other factors can also affect your approval odds.

We’ve collected and analyzed the offer history over the past few years for Capital One's most popular cards and determined the best time to apply for each.

Limited-time offer on the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card: Earn more than $1,000 in travel bonuses with a limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, plus earn 75,000 bonus miles once you spend $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

It's important to note that we'll only discuss publicly available welcome offers. However, you might receive targeted offers that offer more bonus miles or cash back. You can also check for preapproved Capital One offers without affecting your credit score, which may help you find targeted offers that are higher than the publicly available bonus.

Keep in mind that offers may change at any time, and some of those mentioned below may not be available.

The bonus offer values throughout this guide are based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations and are not provided by the credit card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card earns an unlimited 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, plus 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, rental cars and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel.

The card’s modest $95 annual fee, simple earning structure and solid return on everyday spending make it a keeper once you’re approved for it.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture Rewards:

Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening (public offer).

The highest offer we've seen on this card allowed new cardholders to earn up to 100,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offers more than 75,000 miles — whether through additional miles or a travel credit — it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

The Capital One Venture Business card is a straightforward option for business owners who want consistent travel rewards without having to track bonus categories. With a $95 annual fee, it offers simple earning rates, easy-to-use credits and flexible redemption options that help offset the cost year after year.

While it doesn’t come with premium perks like lounge access, its simplicity and solid earning structure make it a reliable long-term choice for everyday business spending.

The Venture Business's launch offer of up to 150,000 miles (75,000 miles after spending $7,500 on purchases in the first three months, plus an additional 75,000 miles after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months) is the best offer we've seen so far.

As a recently launched card, the Venture Business has only two bonus offers. Since there’s limited historical data, we recommend applying when the bonus is over 100,000 miles.

With plentiful, easy-to-understand perks, the Capital One Venture X is a no-brainer for all travelers, from luxury seekers to the more budget-minded, and the card practically pays for itself year after year.

Though the card carries a $395 annual fee, it offers a $300 annual credit toward bookings made through Capital One Travel and rewards cardholders with 10,000 bonus miles each account anniversary.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture X:

The highest offer we've seen on this card offered 100,000 bonus miles earned after spending $10,000 on purchases within the first six months of account opening.

When the bonus offer is 75,000 miles or higher, it's a good time to apply.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

The Venture X Business carries the same $395 annual fee as the personal version and offers the same major perks, including a $300 annual travel credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel and access to Capital One and participating Priority Pass lounges. It also carries the same earning rates as the Venture X.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture X Business:

The highest offer we've seen on this card is up to 400,000 bonus miles: Earn 200,000 miles after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus an additional 200,000 miles after spending $150,000 on purchases in the first six months.

When the bonus offer is for more than 150,000 miles, it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

While it comes with fewer perks, the Capital One VentureOne Rewards offers the same great redemption options as its sister cards, the Capital One Venture Rewards and the Capital One Venture X, with no annual fee. You’ll earn a flat 1.25 miles per dollar spent on everyday purchases.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One VentureOne Rewards:

The highest offer we've seen allowed new cardholders to earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 in the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offers more than 20,000 miles — whether through additional miles or a travel credit — it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card

The biggest downsides to cash-back cards are low earning rates and a lack of bonus categories, but that’s definitely not true of the Capital One Savor Cash Rewards.

For no annual fee, the Savor offers strong cash-back earning rates on popular and often overlooked categories, including 3% back on dining, entertainment and popular streaming services.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Savor Cash Rewards:

The highest offer we've seen included a $100 Capital One Travel credit to use in the first year. Plus, new cardholders could receive a $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offer is $250 or more, it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card

The Capital One Quicksilver Cash Rewards is another great card with no annual fee. It earns a reliable 1.5% cash back on all purchases, making it a perfect go-to card for the odd purchase that doesn’t fit in any bonus categories.

While many other cards offer higher earning potential in specific spending categories, this card offers the safety of knowing you’ll earn a solid 1.5% back no matter what you buy.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Quicksilver Cash Rewards:

The highest offer we've seen included a $100 Capital One Travel credit to use in the first year. Plus, new cardholders could receive a $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offer is $200 or higher, it meets our criteria for applying.

The Capital One Spark Cash Plus earns 2% cash back on all purchases and is ideal for business owners who want to earn reliable cash-back rewards on all their expenses. It is worth noting that this is a no-preset-spending-limit card, meaning cardholders must pay off their balances in full each month.

The card has a modest $150 annual fee that can be refunded after spending at least $150,000 in your card anniversary year.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Spark Cash Plus:

When the bonus is $2,000 or higher, it meets our application criteria.

The Capital One Spark Cash earns 5% cash back on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel and 2% cash back on all other purchases. With the flat rate earning structure, the card is ideal for businesses with spending across different categories.

The card has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then a $95 annual fee.

The Spark Cash is a traditional credit card that allows cardholders to carry a balance, offering more flexibility for businesses that don’t want to pay their balance in full each month.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Spark Cash:

The highest welcome offer we've seen on this card is $1,500 in cash back after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

When the bonus exceeds $1,000, it meets our application threshold.

The Capital One Spark Cash Select is a solid option for small-business owners who want to earn straightforward cash-back rewards without paying an annual fee.

The card earns unlimited 1.5% cash back on all purchases, plus 5% cash back on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Spark Cash Select:

The highest welcome offer we've seen on this card is $750 cash back after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

When the bonus exceeds $500, it meets our application threshold.

Learn more: Capital One Spark Cash Select

For several Capital One cards, you won't be eligible if you've received a new cardmember bonus on the same card — or, in some cases, another card in the same family — within the past 48 months. For example, the Venture Rewards terms exclude applicants who have received a new cardmember bonus on the Venture Rewards or Venture X within the past 48 months.

#6065. Why Ultra-Long-Haul Flights Are Easier On An Aircraft Than Short Hops

Services like Qatar Airways' flight from Doha to Auckland and Singapore Airlines' route from Singapore to New York are among the most challenging flights in the world. They push modern aircraft to their limits, testing their range, performance, and fuel burn like no other. There's been a noticeable increase in ultra-long-haul flights in recent years, driven by the arrival of new aircraft like the Airbus A350 and Boeing 787 Dreamliner, which are more capable and efficient than earlier widebodies.

However, while these flights push planes to their technical limits, they aren't particularly physically demanding on the aircraft. Longer flights are actually much less stressful on the airframe and the engines than operating multiple shorter services in a given day with few breaks in between. Naturally, multiple factors go into how stressed an aircraft is during a flight, and time between flights also matters.

The lifespan of large transport aircraft is really determined by two measurements: cycles and hours. The hours metric is as the word implies, while cycles measure the number of times an aircraft is pressurized and depressurized. This roughly corresponds to the number of flights the aircraft takes, although airliners do occasionally operate flights without fully pressurizing the cabin (these are almost always ferry flights flown when the aircraft has a pressurization issue).

Widebody aircraft operating long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights tend to rack up hours very quickly, while short-haul airliners rack up cycles quickly. However, while hours are one measure of an airframe's lifespan, the number of cycles/flights operated is a more important metric for determining how stressed the aircraft is overall. Operating multiple flights means the landing gear and brakes are used for multiple landings, while the fuel and hydraulic systems also wear with each flight.

In addition, each flight involves the engines being pushed to takeoff power and, typically, the reverse thrusters being activated upon landing (this doesn't occur with every landing, but it occurs onalmost every landing). This puts strain on the engines, whereas an aircraft operating a long-haul or ultra-long-haul flight only performs one takeoff and one landing. The number of hours an aircraft flies certainly stresses the airframe, but its cycles and the number of flights it takes physically stress the plane even more.

Hawaiian Airlines currently operates 19 717-200s. These planes are used exclusively to operate between the Hawaiian islands, which means that they routinely operate eight, nine, 10, or even 11 flights per day. Most of these flights last under 40 minutes, so they're not racking up hours as quickly as a typical widebody. However, despite the short length of these routes, the Hawaiian interisland operations are considered some of the most demanding in the world.

The aircraft's engines are routinely pushed to takeoff power, then reverse thrust is used on the runway, and then this process is repeated multiple times per day. The engines are constantly being used and rarely have time to cool down. The landing gear and brakes are used frequently, and short turnaround times mean the plane rarely rests. What's more, the environment exposes the aircraft to salt particles in the air, raising corrosion concerns and increasing stress on the airframe.

737 MAX 7, 737 MAX 8, 737 MAX 9, 737 MAX 10

One of Hawaiian's biggest challenges was determining how these aging planes would be replaced. The engines on newer types like the A321neo and 737 MAX would not take kindly to the constant stress, while their fuel efficiency would provide little benefit. Ultimately, Alaska Air Group (which now owns the Hawaiian brand) opted to use older 737-800s from Alaska's fleet to replace the 717s, presumably scheduling extra downtime due to the aircraft's size and to allow the planes to rest more.

The A350's reputation as a 'passenger favorite' masks a more complex truth for flight crews, whose rest experiences can vary widely.

Hour and cycle limits are mainly used for pressurized aircraft because of the stresses pressurization introduces on the airframe. While other components of the aircraft also get stressed, pressurization is one of the largest stress factors. Each time the aircraft is pressurized, the fuselage expands slightly as the high pressure air inside the cabin pushes the fuselage against the low-pressure air outside. Over time, this can fatigue the fuselage, potentially resulting in microscopic cracks.

Regularly scheduled maintenance inspections uncover any potential fatigue cracks before they become a safety issue, but the pressurization cycle nonetheless puts significant stress on the fuselage. The pressurization cycle and these stress forces were a major factor in two mid-flight breakups of the de Havilland Comet in the 1950s, the world's first jet airliner. While it was not the first pressurized aircraft, no other airliner flew so high, and the intense forces from pressurization cycles fatigued the fuselage far faster than anticipated.

Metallic fuselages are particularly susceptible to the stress forces caused by pressurization, while newer carbon-composite designs are much stronger. This has allowed manufacturers to lower cabin altitudes by using higher-pressure air, which would ordinarily require a much heavier metal fuselage due to the added strengthening needed. Meanwhile, some business jets have even lower cabin altitudes while flying higher than airliners, which is justifiable as weight and fuel burn are less of a concern in private aviation.

Aircraft are designed to serve for upwards of 30 or even 35 years, so aircraft engineers design them with a specific service life in mind that covers typical usage across multiple decades. Manufacturers perform fatigue analysis to establish safe limits and inspection intervals for the aircraft, while working with regulators to determine the aircraft's lifespan. This is designed around the plane's intended mission, with widebodies and narrowbodies having vastly different hours-to-cycles ratios.

In addition to the aircraft's overall lifespan, various components may have their own maintenance intervals, with engines in particular largely on their own schedules. Overall, aircraft designers set goals for the expected service life of the aircraft and its components, and then work diligently to achieve them. In addition, the original limits set for an aircraft are often increased by the manufacturer later in the type's service life, usually via an upgrade that can be retrofitted onto pre-existing examples.

The A320 was originally designed with a service limit of 60,000 flight hours or 48,000 cycles, whichever occurs first. Later on, Airbus was able to increase these limits to 120,000 hours or 60,000 cycles, whichever occurs first. The 767, meanwhile, is designed with a limit of 50,000 cycles, fewer than the A320, but more hours. In addition, some aircraft types are converted to freighters later in their lives, and these projects often come with post-conversion limits as well.

Is there a possibility that Boeing will make an extended-range version of the 787 Dreamliner?

An aircraft's age is often quoted in terms of years, but this doesn't have much of an impact on its actual remaining lifespan. While age can determine factors such as reliability and which parts need to be used, planes can easily operate for upwards of 40 years if they don't exceed their hour and cycle limits. Instead, however, planes are largely retired for economic reasons, as maintaining an old aircraft that has operated for decades is possible but rarely cheap.

As aircraft become older, they become less reliable, and maintenance costs tend to rise. In addition, airliners require multiple types of maintenance overhauls, including what are often dubbed 'D checks', where basically the entire aircraft is taken apart, which come at a huge cost. Older aircraft also burn more fuel than newer ones, which makes it much more expensive to operate aging planes. Oftentimes, airlines will retire their oldest planes right before their next major overhaul, and then they get sent for scrapping.

Because aircraft are retired for economic reasons, it's actually rare to see them near their service limitations. What's more, aging planes tend to be used less often towards the end of their lives due to their high operating costs, which further slows the pace at which the aircraft approaches its service limits. As such, some aircraft remain in service for upwards of 40 years with small cargo operators and in nations such as Iran, as well as older 737s and A320s that are nearly 40 years old, since they remain within their hour and cycle limits.

#6064. American Grows Maintenance Footprint in Miami

A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

The airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

“Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”

American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

#6063. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.
