#6062. 5 Widebody Aircraft That Define Commercial Aviation In 2026

The Boeing 787 Dreamliner and Airbus A350 are becoming the backbone of long-haul aviation; however, they are far from the only widebody aircraft shaping the industry in 2026. While Boeing continues to prepare its delayed 777X for entry into service, airlines are ordering more Airbus A330neos and investing heavily in aircraft that were once expected to disappear from their fleets, including the Airbus A380.

Emirates alone has 270 Boeing 777Xs on order, yet expects to operate some A380s until around 2041. These five aircraft families therefore serve very different markets, from thinner nonstop routes to congested hubs where airlines need more than 500 seats per flight. Purchase prices, delivery availability, capacity, and route networks are therefore just as important as technology. Here are five widebody families that illustrate those decisions in 2026.

The A380 is the only aircraft on this list no longer in production. Airbus delivered the final example in 2021 as airlines increasingly favored smaller twin-engine widebodies. Its capacity and four engines make it difficult to operate profitably on thinner routes, but more attractive where airport slots are limited and demand is high. At congested hubs, airlines cannot simply add departures when demand grows.

Emirates is by far the largest A380 operator, with a fleet of 116 aircraft, while British Airways, Singapore Airlines, Qantas, and several other carriers continue using the type. In spring 2026, roughly 190 A380s were in airline fleets worldwide, meaning Emirates alone accounted for well over half of the total. Many operators of the A380 have found that their existing superjumbos retain their value and replacing an A380 with a smaller jet reduces available seats unless airlines secure more slots.

Its upper deck accommodates large business class cabins and an onboard lounge, while the first class showers remain a distinctive feature. Emirates has committed billions of dollars to refurbishing its existing fleet, including fitting Premium Economy cabins on the A380. In July, the airline announced that its wider retrofit program had reached 100 aircraft across the A380 and 777 fleets, including 47 A380s. It is also converting two-class A380s into three-class aircraft with Premium Economy.

Qantas plans to begin retiring its remaining superjumbos from 2028 as its long-haul fleet expands. Emirates, in contrast, expects to operate some aircraft until around 2041, as its massive global network continues to support the A380's capacity. With no direct replacement for a 500-seat double-decker currently in production, the airline will have to balance rising maintenance costs against the value of keeping that capacity available at slot-constrained airports.

The A330neo has attracted fewer orders than the 787 or A350, but offers a combination the newer aircraft cannot always match: relatively low acquisition costs, substantial capacity, and an established airframe. The A330-900 is powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 engines and features aerodynamic improvements, including larger composite winglets. Airbus says it burns 14% less fuel per seat than the previous-generation A330.

According to aviation consultancy Visual Approach, new A330-900s were being delivered at prices around $120 million in late 2025, compared with more than $160 million for a Boeing 787-9 and over $170 million for an A350. These market estimates, rather than list prices, help explain its appeal on routes that do not need the performance of a more expensive aircraft. Lower ownership costs can be particularly valuable for leisure airlines and operators with seasonal demand. When an A350’s additional range goes unused, its higher purchase price can be difficult to justify.

The Five Largest A330-900neo Operators In November 2026

Airbus says the A330neo shares up to 95% of its airframe spare parts by part number with the older A330ceo, reducing investments in spares, tooling, and technical training. Airlines such as Delta, TAP Air Portugal, and Condor have demonstrated the aircraft's versatility across different long-haul business models. However, the Trent 7000 has also faced durability challenges, with engine time on wing becoming a concern for operators and a factor in the aircraft’s overall economics. Moreover, seating density and flight length also influence whether its economics compare favorably with newer designs.

The aircraft's position has strengthened further through several orders in 2026. Delta ordered another 16 A330-900s in January, Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) committed to 18 in June, and leasing company Avolon placed an order for 35 in October.

Delta is currently the world's largest A330-900 operator, while Cathay Pacific has the most on order.

More than 30 years after entering service, the 777 remains important for long-haul passenger and cargo operations. The 777-300ER combines high capacity with enough range for most major intercontinental routes. Emirates continues to operate the world's largest 777 fleet, and the type remains central to its Dubai-based connecting network alongside the Airbus A380. Unlike the larger superjumbo, the 777 serves markets that cannot fill 500 seats per departure while still providing premium and cargo capacity.

In November 2025, Emirates ordered another 65 Boeing 777-9s, bringing its total 777X commitment to 270 aircraft. The commitment underscores the role of high-capacity twinjets in its future fleet. The 777-9 will be the world’s largest twin-engine passenger jet, combining additional capacity with more efficient engines and a new composite wing. However, the program has suffered repeated delays, and Boeing's latest October 2026 update still targets first delivery in 2027. However, German flag-carrier Lufthansa, the type's launch customer, has already been planning its summer 2027 schedule without relying on the type.

Existing older 777s will therefore remain important longer than anticipated. Emirates, for example, is refurbishing its cabins with updated business class and premium economy products, maintaining their commercial appeal while replacement aircraft are delayed. Refurbishing aircraft also postpones the expense of buying replacements.

Boeing has hundreds of 777-9 orders, but its first deliveries are years late. Here are the airlines waiting to replace their 777s.

The A350 is becoming the flagship of airlines across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Its composite structure and modern engines deliver lower fuel consumption than many older widebodies. The larger A350-1000 also competes directly with the Boeing 777-300ER and upcoming 777-9. Its Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines and higher capacity make it particularly suitable for airlines replacing older large widebodies while maintaining a premium-heavy cabin.

Lufthansa took delivery of its first A350-1000 on November 10, with a 300-seat configuration featuring its Allegris cabin. Delta Air Lines, Air Canada, and Riyadh Air have also committed to the variant. The A350 family had secured more than 1,620 orders by the end of August, according to Airbus. The delayed 777X has made the A350-1000 an available alternative, although other factors also influence fleet decisions.

The A350's capabilities are particularly visible in Qantas' Project Sunrise program. The airline is preparing 12 specially modified A350-1000ULRs to operate nonstop flights from Sydney to London, beginning in October 2027, followed by New York in 2028. They will feature just 238 seats across four classes, a particularly low density for the type. The additional fuel capacity needed for these 20-hour-plus flights means that Qantas is prioritizing range and passenger comfort over the much higher seating capacity the aircraft could otherwise offer. In November, a Project Sunrise test aircraft completed a record-breaking 24-hour, 24-minute flight from Melbourne to Toulouse.

The 787 Dreamliner combines relatively modest capacity with the range needed to connect smaller long-haul markets. According to Boeing, the aircraft family has enabled airlines to open more than 530 previously unserved nonstop routes, including flights where a larger widebody might struggle to fill enough seats. This allows network carriers to launch services that previously required a connecting flight through another hub. It is particularly valuable when demand is spread across many destinations rather than a few trunk routes.

The 787-8 serves smaller markets, the 787-9 balances capacity and range, and the 787-10 provides more seats where its shorter range is sufficient. The largest operators include All Nippon Airways (ANA), United Airlines, American Airlines, and Qatar Airways. Its composite fuselage also allows lower cabin altitude and higher humidity than traditional aluminum aircraft. These improvements contribute to the Dreamliner’s passenger appeal.

In March, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approved higher maximum takeoff weights for the 787-9 and 787-10. According to Boeing, the upgrade gives the 787-9 approximately 10,000 lb (4,540 kg) of additional takeoff weight, allowing it to carry more payload or fly over 300 nautical miles (560 km) farther. The larger 787-10 gains around 14,000 lb (6,350 kg), potentially extending its range by more than 400 nautical miles (740 km).

#6060. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

Now, here's the hotel news you need to know about from this week.

Hyatt is expanding its lifestyle footprint with the opening of the first Andaz in Australia. The Andaz Gold Coast, located in sunny Queensland, will have 202 rooms and plans to "redefine coastal luxury through a distinctive blend of expressive Australian design and immersive experiences inspired by the people, places, and creative spirit of the Gold Coast," according to a statement from Hyatt. The property is near the beaches of Broadbeach, and features a series of bars and restaurants, plus a lively pool club offering live music and community-focused barbecues.

Also in Queensland, Brisbane will welcome a Park Hyatt in 2031, ahead of the 2032 Brisbane Olympics. Brisbane is one of my favorite cities, so I can't wait (though I'll have to) for the 201-room property not far from Suncorp Stadium, which will host a series of soccer and rugby events. Many details about the property are still under wraps, but if it's even half as great as the Park Hyatt Sydney, we know it'll be a great hotel.

If you haven't had the chance to visit Houston, I can't recommend it enough. The city is home to diverse cultures, incredible food and the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo, one of the biggest rodeos in the world. If you find yourself in Beyoncé's hometown, consider a stay at the JW Marriott Houston Downtown, which just completed a years-long head-to-toe remodel. The hotel now features fresh rooms, including 56 new rooms, a redesigned lobby restaurant and a total revamp of the hotel's food and beverage offerings.

Monti, my favorite neighborhood in Rome, feels like stepping back in time. Or, at least into a movie set, thanks to its beautiful vine-covered walls, cobblestone streets and lively energy near the Colosseum. In 2028, it'll also be home to Hortus Monti Rome, part of Hilton's upscale LXR Hotels & Resorts. The hotel is spread across six historic Umbertine-era buildings, according to a statement from Hilton and features a central garden, a spa, bars and restaurants and more.

Until then, Hilton fans should check into Rome Cavalieri, one of the most popular Waldorf Astoria hotels in the world.

The Coke versus Pepsi debate is a serious one, and people tend to have strong opinions about which is better. While I'm a Diet Dr. Pepper fanatic myself, it looks like Hyatt is doubling down on its relationship with Pepsi. The company just renewed its contract, making PepsiCo the preferred beverage partner across 700 Hyatt properties in the United States. The agreement also extends to certain PepsiCo snack products.

Earlier this year, Marriott ousted Pepsi and made Coca-Cola its "global beverage partner across several categories, including carbonated soft drinks and a growing range of hydration and functional beverages."

#6058. How Much It Costs Emirates To Keep Its Airbus A380 Fleet Flying In 2026

Emirates is pouring billions of dollars into cabin overhauls and spending tens of thousands of dollars an hour on fuel and maintenance for an Airbus A380 fleet that other airlines are retiring early. The carrier does not disclose what it spends to keep each superjumbo flying, so the true price tag of sustaining the world's largest passenger airliner is still hidden behind industry estimates, unscheduled technical directives, and a sprawling refurbishment program.

At the center of that commitment is Emirates President Tim Clark, whose bet on the A380 stretches well into the next decade even as replacement aircraft deliveries slip and fuel markets stay volatile. How much does keeping the A380 fleet flying in 2026 actually cost Emirates, and what keeps the airline paying the bill?

Industry estimates based on 2026 figures, place total A380 operating costs between $40,000 and $55,000 per flight hour, depending on fuel prices and mission length. According to Golden Epaulets Aviation, fuel accounts for $20,000 to $26,000 per flight hour; airport and navigation fees run $5,000 to $9,000; maintenance and engineering reach $8,000 to $12,000; and crew adds $4,000 to $6,000.

Fuel assumptions across aviation analyses vary sharply, showing how sensitive hourly burn is to crude and jet fuel pricing. While Golden Epaulets Aviation puts A380 fuel burn at $20,000 to $26,000 per flight hour in 2026, estimates put it at $11,500 per hour, and energy markets have faced upward pressure since the Iran conflict began in 2026.

For the A380, engineering and maintenance bring a massive penalty that twin-engine widebodies avoid. Separate industry estimates put A380 maintenance alone at $6,000 to $8,000 per flight hour, reflecting the extra inspections, parts, and shop visits required across four engines rather than just two.

Emirates is committing $5 billion to overhaul the cabin interiors of 219 aircraft, which, when broken down, comprise 110 A380s and 109 777s. It is natural to see such a move as pointless with new-generation aircraft on the way, but delays to these new aircraft deliveries have led the airline to refresh existing widebodies, because retiring them is no longer a viable option. Originally scoped to cover 67 A380s and 53 777s, the program expanded in May 2024 by adding 43 more A380s and 28 more 777s as replacement jet timelines stretched out.

Each A380 refurbishment comes with roughly 33,000 work hours over 21 days and more than 4,000 new parts, according to AeroTime. Across 44 months of work through April 2026, Emirates had completed 100 aircraft, 47 A380s and 53 777s, using 4.4 million work hours, with more than half of the 219-aircraft total projected to finish by December 2026.

In May, Emirates completed its first retrofit of a two-class A380, and a subsequent phase covering 60 A380s and 51 Boeing 777s began in August. When all is done, Emirates will be left with a fully refreshed fleet that meets the high demands of its most loyal customers, but keeping so many cabins out of line for three-week overhauls makes this cabin modernization a multi-year capital and hangar balancing act for the carrier.

The carrier is taking ownership of its double-decker fleet.

Of course, there are the scheduled checks and routine hourly burn, but unexpected technical mandates added sharp, unbudgeted costs to operating the A380. In October, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered turbine seal replacements on certain Engine Alliance GP7200 engines, the powerplant fitted to most Emirates A380s, after an uncontained engine failure forced an A380 to abort a takeoff.

AeroTime estimated that complying with the directive could cost up to $528,150 per affected engine, creating an immediate financial overhang whenever covered units come due for work. The reality is, however, that exact counts of affected engines across Emirates's fleet are not public, so it is important to keep in mind that the per-engine estimate highlights unit-level exposure and does not necessarily translate into a confirmed fleetwide bill.

Structural checks also interrupted availability earlier in the year, showing that airframe aging brings its own surprise bills. In June 2026, Airbus conducted inspections on 16 A380s, 15 of those being operated by Emirates, after cracks turned up in a key wing component, which resulted in unscheduled inspection work on high-utilization widebodies.

Spending heavily on an airframe only pays off when the jet is generating revenue, though interestingly, nearly 30 Emirates A380s sat out of service at some point in 2026 due to cabin overhauls, routine maintenance, or temporary operational changes, as reported by Arabian Gulf Business Insight. Even with that downtime, Emirates expects roughly 110 A380s to be in active service by the end of 2026, showing how much capacity the airline can still field once aircraft cycle back onto the schedule instead of leaving the entire double-decker subfleet parked.

Temporary schedule trims and flight reductions in 2026 show how quickly fleet availability ripples through Emirates's network from Dubai. When widebodies step off the line for maintenance, refurbishment, or operational adjustments, planners will need to trim frequencies or reshuffle aircraft assignments because stretching every remaining superjumbo indefinitely across long-haul sectors just doesn't work in this kind of scenario.

Every parked or temporarily sidelined A380 carries an opportunity cost alongside direct upkeep, tying up high-capacity seats during peak travel windows when demand is high. Getting those grounded frames back into rotation and keeping the active core flying reliably is central to turning high fixed and maintenance spending into ticket revenue.

While other airlines have parked the A380, Emirates remains committed to the double-decker.

It is clear today that the A380 is not something that the vast majority of airlines want, but Emirates still accepts the steep hourly burn, multi-billion-dollar cabin spending, and sudden technical bills. The reason for this is that Emirates President Tim Clark regards the Airbus A380 as "the most profitable asset in our fleet." Where other airlines have widely regarded the four-engine superjumbo as an oversized relic that is expensive to fill and costly to power, Emirates sees its high-capacity footprint as a core commercial engine when demand peaks on major trunk routes.

No aircraft currently in production matches the A380's passenger capacity in a single airframe, which explains why Emirates intends to fly the type until roughly 2041 despite persistent four-engine cost pressure. Replacing hundreds of double-decker seats at slot-constrained airports with smaller twin-engine widebodies would mean that Emirates has to add more frequencies or leave high-demand departures with fewer seats to sell during peak periods.

Even so, keeping an aging four-engine type flying toward 2041 is not a free pass from economic friction, since fuel volatility and higher maintenance intensity continually test that profitability thesis. Emirates holds on to that massive revenue-generating capacity, but something naturally has to give. That being the high per-hour costs and long-horizon airframe support, which will continue to be the defining trade-off behind Emirates's willingness to pay for the A380.

Whether the A380 can stay as a commercial winner for Emirates through the next decade is really dependent on how fuel prices behave after the 2026 Iran conflict shock and how quickly replacement widebody deliveries arrive. The higher-than-ever jet fuel costs hit four-engine economics harder than twin-engine competitors, while ongoing OEM delivery delays determine how long Emirates must lean on refurbished double-deckers to hold capacity across major trunk routes without losing market share at slot-constrained hubs.

December 2026 offers an immediate checkpoint on that trajectory, as Emirates aims to have more than half of its 219-aircraft cabin retrofit program completed and roughly 110 A380s in active service by year-end. Meeting those targets, all while managing unscheduled engine and airframe checks, from turbine seal directives to structural inspections, will be what shows whether Emirates can keep its biggest revenue earner ahead of its rising upkeep as aircraft cycle through hangars.

The question that many still have is how smoothly a replacement aircraft eventually arrives, which at the moment is considered to be the Boeing 777X, and how stubborn fuel and maintenance expenses prove over the coming years. Whatever the future holds, it ultimately will decide whether keeping the A380 flying until about 2041 stays an asset or turns into a heavier burden. For now, Emirates is betting that unmatched single-airframe scale outweighs higher per-hour and refurbishment costs, even as every shift in oil prices or delivery schedules tests the margin on that strategy.

#6057. Delta Outage Delays Hundreds of Flights

A problem with one of Delta’s weight-and-balance systems delayed hundreds of flights Sunday, with backups most acute at the nation’s busiest airport.

According to FlightAware, Delta delayed over 2,100 flights Sunday and canceled 274.

Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport was the hardest hit, with about 700 flights delayed, though not all were Delta connections.

Delta said in a statement that its employees were using manual workarounds for baggage processing. It also said it would rebook customers on the next available flight and provide meals and hotel rooms where needed.

The FAA said on X that the problem was specific to Delta and had nothing to do with the agency’s air traffic control system, which crashed on Nov. 13.

Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information. https://t.co/q4Fc59VMYg

The outage was resolved Sunday afternoon.

As of Monday morning, Delta’s delay rate was down to 6%.

While resolved fairly quickly, the system failure could hardly have come at a worse time. Millions of Americans are flying this week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, and there are concerns that technology outages could again snarl air traffic during the busiest time of the year. The single busiest day for air travel is expected to be Sunday, Nov. 29, after Thanksgiving.

Let’s go through all the types of airport lounges that are part of the American Express Global Lounge Collection.

As a cardmember of either the personal or business Platinum card, including authorized users with additional Platinum cards but not authorized users with companion Platinum cards, you’ll get access to most eligible lounge networks by showing your eligible card and government-issued identification, plus a valid boarding pass.

However, each lounge network has different access requirements and guest policies, so let’s look at each.

Centurion Lounges are Amex’s flagship airport lounges. They offer a staffed bar, meals, ample nonalcoholic drinks, high-speed Wi-Fi and various seating options.

Some Centurion Lounges also provide complimentary amenities like family rooms.

15 Centurion Lounges are open in the U.S.:

Platinum Card and Business Platinum Card members may only access the Centurion Lounge within three hours of their flight’s scheduled departure. To gain access, you’ll need to provide a same-day, confirmed boarding pass, your eligible Amex card, and your government-issued identification.

After you have used all 10 visits, additional visits to a Delta Sky Club can be bought for $50 per visit, or $25 per visit for Delta Sky Club 'Grab and Go' locations. Delta's Sky Club terms and conditions state:

A visit is an entry to one or more Delta Sky Clubs or usage of the Delta Sky Club "Grab and Go" feature, at one or more airports, for a period of up to 24 hours starting upon the first Delta Sky Club entry or Grab and Go usage.

A single visit permits usage of Delta Sky Club(s) in multiple airports during the 24-hour period. For example, if you visit a Delta Sky Club in different airports on a trip, entry into one or more of these Clubs will be considered part of the same visit as long as these additional entries occur within 24 hours of the first Delta Sky Club entry.

Luckily, cardmembers with connecting itineraries or a brief layover during the same day won't have to worry about whether it's worth it to enter a Sky Club and burn a visit if they have already entered a Sky Club prior to their departure.

However, if you spend $75,000 or more on your Amex Platinum Card or Business Platinum Card during a calendar year (January through December), you can unlock unlimited Sky Club access through the end of the next program year (February through January).

#6054. JetBlue Airbus A321neo Still Grounded At LAX After Late-Night Tail Strike Caught On Camera

A two-year-old JetBlue Airbus A321neo remains grounded at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) after striking its tail during a late-night go-around on November 22. The aircraft had pitched up to climb away when the underside of its rear fuselage scraped the runway, sending sparks flying on a live broadcast from Airline Videos.

Originating from Boston (BOS), tail number N2193J was attempting to land on Runway 25L at 11:44 PM local time when the crew initiated the ill-fated go-around. Following the contact, the pilots climbed out safely, repositioned for a second approach to Runway 25L, and landed without further incident roughly 16 minutes later at 12:01 AM.

While the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) logged a preliminary incident report noting the go-around tail strike, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has not yet listed a formal investigation while the extent of the physical damage is assessed. The plane involved is a 2-year-old Airbus A321-271NX named 'StateMint Piece,' which was delivered to JetBlue in December 2024. Its scheduled return leg as Flight B6524 to New York-JFK (JFK) at 2:30 PM today was canceled.

The last tail strike by a JetBlue-operated aircraft occurred in February at San Francisco International Airport (SFO). That A321neo, tail N2188J, was also flying into the West Coast from Boston. Operating as Flight B62233, it struck its tail on Runway 28L at SFO during landing. According to the NTSB final report via AeroCorner, the jet bounced upon touchdown, and the first officer pulled the sidestick fully aft while applying go-around power, causing substantial damage to the lower fuselage.

The Aviation Safety Network reports on another tail strike by a plane flown by JetBlue in 2022. That Airbus A320, tail N760JB, was damaged during takeoff out of Hayden, Colorado, due to confusion with local general aviation traffic and pilot error. While attempting to coordinate with a Beechcraft B300 King Air that was inbound, the crew performed a rapid departure and rotated 24 knots under speed while also striking the tail of the jet.

Fortunately, in all three instances of recent tail strike mishaps for JetBlue air crews, no injuries were reported aboard any of the planes. While formal findings are still pending from Sunday night's incident, the video showing a shower of sparks during the late-night go-around means that there will be repairs to paint, scraped-off rivets, and potentially failed fuselage panels. • Lower fuselage protrusions, like heated drain masts and VHF/transponder antennas, may have also been sheared off or crushed.

Following the accident at SFO, tail N2188J suffered what the NTSB described as substantial damage. Post-flight inspections documented significant scraping and abrasion across the lower aft skin, along with damage to a pitot tube. As the jet bounced twice before the first officer pulled full aft sidestick, the impact required major repairs to restore the lower fuselage skin and support structure before the aircraft could return to service.

Similarly, tail N760JB saw substantial abrasion damage across multiple fuselage frames, according to NTSB post-mishap inspections. Notably, the crew did not initially realize they had struck the tail until air traffic control alerted them at 31,000 feet (9,448.8 meters), prompting an immediate diversion to Denver. Since the tail-strike damage may have compromised pressurized sections of the rear fuselage, the aircraft cannot safely fly at high altitude and must be repaired on-site or flown at low altitude to a maintenance base.

The A321neo is now a highly common sight.

For tail N2193J, the process is well underway to find the damage and correct it so that the plane can return to service safely. Immediately after landing, maintenance crews would have pulled the Cockpit Voice Recorder and Flight Data Recorder. The FAA and NTSB will analyze exact pitch angles, airspeed, and stick inputs at the critical phase of flight when the mishap occurred.

If the damage is considered to be superficial within the allowable limits for skin abrasion set by Airbus, mechanics at LAX can install an aerodynamic 'scab patch,' or doubler. If the inspection finds substantial damage, then engineers will need to be involved to develop a custom repair scheme.

Should that be necessary, the plane will fly under 10,000 feet (3,048 meters) per a 'ferry permit' to make its way to a proper maintenance, repair, and overhaul depot that can handle the scope of work. As for the pilots, the typical procedure is focused on identifying safety failures and retraining rather than punishment. That is provided that the accident was not a result of misconduct.

#6053. Storms on Both Coasts Threaten Thanksgiving Travel

Powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S. during the single busiest week of the year.

Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. These regions are home to some of the nation’s busiest airports, through which millions of American travelers will pass this week en route to visit family and friends for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

In the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday. A much stronger storm is expected to develop in the Gulf of Mexico between Monday and Tuesday, impact parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Wednesday, and slam into the New York metro area and New England on Thanksgiving Day.

According to an advisory from the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center, strong wind gusts up to 50 mph will be felt from the Carolinas to Maine. Flooding and beach erosion could be seen in coastal areas due to the already high tides.

WPC has initiated Key Messages for a Thanksgiving Coastal Storm that is expected to impact the U.S. East Coast. pic.twitter.com/pdQuU4U4yG

Americans traveling from, through, or to these areas should prepare for the possibility of flooded roads, damage from high winds, and power outages, the agency said.

NYC Emergency Management said Sunday that the storm could bring gusts of 40 to 45 mph and about one to two inches of rain to the city.

For New York and New England, the storm will be at its strongest Thursday evening. Parts of the Adirondacks and northern New England could see ice and snow mixed in with rain.

In California, Oregon, and Washington, residents still recovering from flooding last week could be hit again by rain and strong winds. A new system is expected to move in Tuesday and Wednesday; combined with the “king tides,” the storm could cause flooding up and down the West Coast.

The impact is expected to be most severe between Portland, Oregon, and San Francisco. San Francisco’s mayor said residents should take the forecasts seriously and consider not traveling for the holiday.

The Sierra Nevada, meanwhile, will see fresh snow, meteorologists said.

Over six million people are expected to fly within the U.S. this week for Thanksgiving. The surge is already underway, with many carriers adding flights to accommodate the increased traffic. American Airlines earlier this month projected its busiest Thanksgiving week since before the COVID-19 pandemic; that prediction could hold true for other U.S. airlines as well.

AirlineGeeks will continue to monitor weather conditions and provide updates as the week progresses.

Even in destinations that are overall very safe, petty theft is a risk. For instance, many European cities are pickpocketing hotspots, and crowded tourist attractions like Christmas markets make ideal hunting grounds for thieves.

Thankfully, there are steps you can take to protect yourself. I’ve gathered real-life anecdotes from my fellow travelers at TPG so you know what to look for, and our top tips to help you protect yourself.

The first and easiest precaution you can take is to minimize your loss if you do get robbed.

That means leaving your flashy jewelry or designer-brand luggage at home, as these can often attract thieves. And be sure to make copies of crucial documents and store them in a safe digital place, where you can easily access them if your hard copies get lost.

What about travel insurance? Some policies may cover theft, so check the coverage offered by your credit card. You may want to consider buying additional coverage for particularly costly items.

This one can be tricky, but do your best not to advertise your status as a tourist. In Europe, for instance, dressing in neutral clothing can help you blend in with the locals (meanwhile, bright colors and American sports apparel scream “foreigner”).

Check a map and figure out where you’re going before leaving your hotel to avoid wandering around looking clueless. Familiarize yourself with your destination’s public transport system; thieves often prowl transportation hubs in search of tourists who are out of their element.

The more distracted you are, the easier it is to get separated you from your valuables. Instead of getting absorbed in your phone, keep your gaze up and walk with purpose. Plus, this will help you soak in your surroundings and make the most of your trip.

Public transportation is a pickpocket’s playground, especially lines that cover tourist draws like Rome’s notorious 64 bus and Lisbon’s iconic yellow Tram 28.

Senior editor Lyndsey Matthews says, “When I was 11, I was in London and saw two teens try to pickpocket my grandma on the way out of the Tube.” Thankfully, all they got was some dirty tissues and seashells.

Keep your bags close and in sight while riding public transport. If you’re carrying a daypack, turn it around and carry it on your chest with the straps looped around your shoulders. Be particularly cautious at train, tram and subway stops, where thieves can dash on, grab your suitcase and bolt before the doors shut again.

Thieves often work together, with one creating a spectacle or disturbance — a spilled drink, an argument, a stumble on the metro — while the other preys on distracted bystanders.

Senior editor Colin Hogan once lost his wallet to a pickpocket in Montreal: “She was working alongside a street performer, and as the performer would gather people into a circle around him to view the performance, she would come behind and steal things from bags or pockets while they were distracted.”

If something happens, resist the urge to stare. Stay focused on yourself and your belongings instead.

You’ve probably heard not to leave your wallet in your back pocket, where it will be easy pickings. But skilled thieves can navigate front pockets with ease, or snatch purses and disappear into the crowd before you can blink.

Lead writer Katie Genter has a relative who got robbed on public transportation in Paris: “She was carrying one of those huge purse bags without a zipper on top,” she says, which would be child’s play for most pickpockets.

To reduce your risk, stick to bags that zip closed, and consider clipping the zippers together for an added layer of protection. Opt for a crossbody bag or fanny pack, which is harder to snatch than a shoulder bag, or a money belt you can keep under your clothes.

As travelers have gotten smarter, so have criminals.

One popular tactic is to slice through the strap of a crossbody bag, then make off with it. Director of content strategy Carly Helfand says, “I’ve had my bag sliced from the bottom on the Prague metro and the phone stolen out of it!”

Consider investing in a theft-resistant bag made of tougher material that’s harder for thieves to cut into. I’m a big fan of this one, which also has locking zippers, a cut-resistant strap and RFID-blocking credit card slots.

Remember, you don’t need to make your bag impenetrable. Simply making it harder to access is often enough to convince opportunistic thieves to move on in search of easier targets.

It goes without saying to not leave anything valuable at your seat while you run to the restroom or grab napkins from the bar. But thieves may be bold enough to snatch items from right in front of you, or even out of your hands.

Director of UX Research Mindy Pastrovich says that in Cape Town, “my friend was talking to a guy who asked for her number, and when she took out her phone to give it to him, he stole it and ran away.”

Stay aware of your surroundings. Keep a firm grip on your phone or camera when you’re using it (a wrist strap or lanyard can help), and tuck them out of sight when you’re not. If you sit down in any public place, like a hotel lobby or train car, loop your bag strap around your chair leg or clip your suitcase to the luggage rack.

It can be tempting to keep all your valuables on your person, where you can keep track of them constantly. But even the most vigilant travelers can fall prey to clever thieves.

TPG assistant marketing manager Paige Stepanian has a friend who got pickpocketed on the Barcelona metro. “She had her phone in a fanny pack that was at the front of her, facing into a group of friends. It happened so fast, by the time we realized her phone was gone the person who took it was already off the train!”

In fact, your items are generally safer in your hotel room than your day pack. Keep what you need in a money belt or theft-resistant crossbody purse, and leave the rest in your room. It’s always a good idea to leave valuables out of sight, or better yet, lock them in the hotel safe or your suitcase.

Scams and confidence games can take unexpected forms. I recently heard of a couple friends of a friend who, while stopped in an airport, were approached by a man offering to give them directions. Meanwhile, his accomplice was walking off with the travelers’ luggage.

Other scams may involve someone putting jewelry or accessories on you without your permission or handing you a drink you didn’t ask for — then demanding payment later. Be wary of anyone who is overly friendly, and set boundaries politely but firmly.

On a recent trip to Zanzibar, I couldn’t even take a casual stroll on the beach without at least one person trying to give me a tide pool tour — which I’m sure he would have charged handsomely for, had I not resolutely walked off and left him in the shallows.

If you’re traveling by car, never leave valuables in view when you park, even if you think you’ll be right back.

My friend once had her purse stolen from a rental car in Hawaii while she was stopped at a scenic overlook for a quick photo. Not only did she lose all her money, she also had a heck of a time getting home without an ID.

In areas where break-ins are common, it’s a good idea to empty the car and leave the doors unlocked any time you leave. That way, if a thief decides to take a look inside, you won’t have to deal with the cost and headache of repairing a broken window.

When senior content strategist Gabrielle Bernardini was in Cabo, Mexico, a gas station attendant asked her for her credit card. “I gave it to him, and he handed it to someone next to him, who then ran into the convenience store. Next, I got an alert from Amex that about $4,000 was charged to my card.”

Thankfully, she contacted Amex right away and was able to get the fraudulent charge wiped in about a week.

Despite all the horror stories I’ve mentioned, theft is still relatively uncommon. I’ve been to Europe more times than I can count and never had anything stolen (knock on wood).

Following the tips above won’t guarantee you don’t fall victim to petty theft, but it will significantly slash your risk.

#6051. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

#6049. A Japanese WWII Bomber & A Crashed Continental Boeing 727: The Unlikely Wrecks Hidden In A Pacific Jungle

In October and November 2026, I visited the island of Yap in the eastern Pacific. There, I explored an old Japanese Second World War airfield that had been bombed by the United States during the Second World War. Following the war, the jungle regrew and claimed the various abandoned Japanese aircraft wrecks.

Just next to the old, overgrown Japanese airfield is the functioning Yap International Airport. In 1980, Continental Airlines (Air Micronesia) Boeing 727 operating as Flight 614 crashed while landing. The wreck burned out, although all passengers survived. It came to rest just next to a Mitsubishi G4M 'Betty' bomber at the old Japanese airfield.

Since then, the forest has regrown, and visitors can see what remains of a Japanese Second World War bomber and a Continental Boeing 727 lying side-by-side in the jungle as strange bedfellows. The local volunteer pilot, Amos Collins, showed me the two wrecks that I had failed to find by myself.

Today, Yap is one of the islands that make up the independent nation of the Federated States of Micronesia. During the Second World War, it was controlled by Japan under the League of Nations South Seas Mandate. These were islands that Japan had wrestled control of from Germany in the First World War.

The island of Chuuk (Truk) became a major Japanese naval base, while others were heavily defended as strong points to protect the Japanese home islands. Yap was only lightly defended, being far behind the island chains deeper into the Pacific, and it wasn't until later in the Pacific War that Japan hurriedly moved to fortify the island.

The ruins of Japanese Second World War aircraft, guns, and bunkers can be found across the island. I spent days seeking out and exploring them. According to a modern report by the United States Navy, in May 1944, the Japanese commander of the 22nd Air Flotilla at Chuuk issued orders for the 2nd Attack Force and other air groups to be stationed on Yap.

US military sorties later reported 24 Japanese fighter aircraft, six dive bombers, two medium bombers, and six night fighters on Yap. These later took part in counterattacking US efforts to bombard the Mariana Islands (such as Guam). The US Navy drew up a plan to invade the island as it did with others. However, it soon abandoned the idea in favor of bombing, neutralizing, and bypassing it.

Today, visitors can see the remains of many Japanese military aircraft destroyed on the ground at the airfield next to large bomb craters. Some of these wrecks are marked, others are not marked, or the signs have since disappeared. You should note that this is private property and visitors are expected to ask residents permission to explore them.

I found around seven Japanese aircraft, or what remained of them. Here and there on the island, visitors can see the remains of US Vought F4U Corsair fighter planes and propellers of B-24 bombers that came down on the island. I mostly found the Corsair engines and B-24 propellers.

However, one of the most eye-catching wrecks is that of a Mitsubishi G4M medium bomber/torpedo bomber. Japan built a total of 2,435 of these twin-engined, seven-crew bombers. Presumably, this wreck is one of the two medium bombers US reconnaissance identified.

The wreck is located here on Google Maps, around a third of the way down the airstrip (now functioning as a potholed village road). It was the only Japanese wreck I found on the island that has its own dedicated information plaque. The plaque is so overgrown by algae that it's hard to make anything out. Most information plaques are for US military remains on the island.

The unique service undoubtedly has its quirks and eccentricities.

Continental Airlines established much of the infrastructure to provide scheduled air services to the Micronesian islands, which were then managed by the United States under the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. Essentially, the US took over the Japanese South Seas Mandate by another name. Continental set up its Air Micronesia brand to serve the islands.

Eventually, this was all inherited by United Airlines following the merger. In November 1980, an Air Micronesia Boeing 727-92C (registered N18479) departed Saipan bound for Palau with island hopping stopovers in Guam and Yap. At 9:52 AM the aircraft touched down at Yap 13 feet short of runway 07. The Aviation Safety Network writes that:

"The right main landing gear immediately separated from the aircraft. The aircraft gradually veered off the runway and came to rest in the jungle about 1,700 feet beyond the initial touchdown."

The probable cause is given as the captain prematurely reducing thrust in combination with flying a shallow approach slope angle to an improper touchdown aim point. All 73 occupants were evacuated within around a minute of the aircraft coming to rest. Today, the heavily forested nature of the landscape makes it difficult to understand how the aircraft could have skidded without breaking up.

I was shown the Boeing 727 and its neighboring Japanese Betty bomber wreck by the volunteer pilot, Amos Collins, who flies for Pacific Missionary Aviation. Having made friends with Amos and being an aviation journalist, he invited me on the flight and then showed me the wrecks. PMA is a hybrid charity airline operating in Micronesia.

When we visited the bomber and 727, we had just gotten back from a supply flight to the outer Yap island of Ulithi on a Super King Air 200. The Boeing 727 caught fire after coming to a rest.

Collins told me that the fire truck from neighboring Yap International Airport responded, only to find on site that the truck lacked any water. The stricken 727 subsequently burned down completely. He said that the incident remains a joke among the Yap Airport fire crews today. The main section of the aircraft remaining is the tail, including one of its air intakes for the tail-mounted engine.

Collins is the father of five, and he said his children enjoy crawling through and using the air intake as a playground slide. I thought of climbing through it myself but decided against the idea. While it is difficult to make out in the photographs I took, the Boeing 727 and Betty bomber are literally a stone's throw from each other. A few feet (meters) more of skidding the 727 would have destroyed the Betty wreck.

This article will take a look at the utility of US main operating bases and the USAF strategy in the Indo-Pacific.

Only a minority of both aircraft exist today. The Mitsubishi G4M's cockpit is perhaps the best preserved. It still has the two pilots' seats and what is left of the controls. The control panel remains well-preserved, as does the aluminum frame. All rubber or other materials have since disappeared. The tail section is also relatively well-preserved, as is at least one propeller.

It would seem that propellers have been removed from a number of sites over the years by the locals. Some sites do retain their propellers, but there are also very clearly some propellers on display at residents' homes, and two are on display at PMA's hangar. Regarding PMA's propellers, Collins told me they were from a B-24 and B-29 bomber. I don't know where they came from.

Sometimes just tails, sometimes relatively complete

As stated, only the Boeing 727's tail remains in place today. This is well-preserved, although the rest of the aircraft appears to have been destroyed or removed. Some salvageable components and materials were stripped over the decades, but the first consumed much of the forward and mid-fuselage. Various bits of debris can be found scattered throughout the surrounding jungle, but the tail is the main attraction.

The story of warplanes on Yap is not over, and a new chapter may yet be written. The United States retains responsibility for defending the islands; in practice, this also means the US has exclusive military basing rights. In a period of Great Power Competition with China, the US is moving to expand the airport infrastructure and defenses of the islands as part of the Second Island Chain.

Congress has approved funds to significantly expand Yap International Airport as part of the Air Force's Agile Combat Employment doctrine to disperse aircraft from Guam's Andersen Air Force Base in the event of a high-end conflict. When I was there, ground on the project was not yet broken, and heavy machinery had yet to arrive.

Work on Palau's Peleliu Airfield is in full swing. This raises the prospect that in a future high-end conflict, F-35 fighter jets, KC-46A tankers, and other modern US military aircraft could find themselves destroyed on the ground next to Japanese bombers and fighters long-lost in the jungle.

I asked Collins if he was concerned about the US preparing his remote island for war; he answered no. I asked if that was because he wasn't concerned, or if it was because he was committed to the island and there was nothing he could do with great power politics happening around them. If it's better to accept and get on with life. He said the latter.

Several apps and websites let you search across multiple airlines, alliances and programs at once, rather than worrying about the best loyalty program to sift through. Two of our favorites at TPG are: Seats.aero and Point.me.

Seats.aero currently searches more than 20 airline loyalty programs, including major programs like American Airlines AAdvantage, Delta SkyMiles and United MileagePlus. This powerful tool lets you search all these programs simultaneously across multiple routes, dates, classes and transfer partners in seconds. You can also search individual programs across an extended date range to identify available award seats. There are even handy filters so you can limit factors such as the maximum number of points or surcharges.

The platform has also developed several innovative tools to help you find those harder-to-book seats, such as Lufthansa first class, Delta One, All Nippon Airways first class and Qatar Airways Qsuite. You can set alerts across multiple routes, dates, programs and carriers to be notified by text or email if a seat you seek becomes available. There's also an AI Assistant if you don't know where to start.

Point.me searches more than 150 airlines across over 30 loyalty programs, generally checking one departure date at a time. That's particularly useful when you're trying to compare all the ways to book a specific flight, especially through programs Seats.aero doesn't fully support, such as British Airways Club, Iberia Club and Aer Lingus AerClub.

Unlike Seats.aero's cached results, Point.me uses live award searches. It also shows which transferable credit card currencies you can use, highlights applicable transfer bonuses and provides step-by-step instructions for transferring points and completing the booking.

Be aware that neither tool can actually book the ticket for you, so it's still worth confirming the award directly with your chosen airline program before moving any of your valuable transferable points.

Related: These apps and websites make award redemptions easier to find

The major North American airlines have reasonably comprehensive award search engines, so starting with the airline you want to fly is often the simplest option.

However, you'll sometimes find better value through a partner program. Here are some useful places to search.

It's worth comparing prices before booking. American, Delta and United all use dynamic pricing, so the number of miles required for a flight can change considerably depending on the date and demand.

Booking through a partner might save you thousands of points or miles, but don't assume that partner pricing is always fixed.

For example, Aeroplan now uses variable pricing for United-operated awards, so booking the same flight through Air Canada won't necessarily be cheaper than booking directly with United.

European loyalty programs can offer great redemption deals, whether you are taking, say, a business-class flight to Europe for just 40,500 credit card points or an economy flight to London for just 6,000 points.

Here is how to search for the best award availability:

Some of the most aspirational first-class airline products, such as Etihad's A380 Apartments and Emirates' A380 suites, are offered by Middle Eastern airlines.

Here's how to search for award availability.

Emirates first-class awards now come with additional restrictions. Emirates Skywards only allows Silver, Gold and Platinum members to book first-class Classic Rewards. Qantas Frequent Flyer restricts them to Silver members and above, while Aeroplan requires members to hold Aeroplan 35K status or higher to redeem points for Emirates first class.

Related: Emirates first class still wows: Fully enclosed suites and unlimited caviar

Now that you know where to search for award space for your next trip, here are a few tricks to make the process easier.

This is an odd quirk of most award search engines, but you’ll often get different results if you search for your complete itinerary instead of one flight at a time.

If your complete itinerary isn't showing any award availability, try searching for each flight separately. This can help identify which segment is causing the problem, although finding each flight individually doesn't guarantee that the airline can combine them into a single award. The complete journey still needs to meet the program's routing and ticketing rules.

Sometimes, airlines will offer more seats for indirect itineraries than nonstop ones. Why? Airlines believe passengers will pay more for direct fares with cash (compared to indirect ones), so with less demand for connecting itineraries, they may offer additional seats.

Using this married-segment logic in your next search, you may be able to find long-haul, premium-cabin seats you did not think existed. Consider widening your search to connect in another city using a catch-all external tool like Seats.aero.

You might be surprised by the additional availability if you are willing to fly a little farther than your original destination.

However, don't assume you can remove a connecting segment and keep the same award price or availability.

One particularly frustrating issue when booking partner awards is phantom availability. This happens when an airline or search tool displays an award seat that can't actually be booked.

Unfortunately, this remains a problem across several major loyalty programs.

Before transferring points, select the exact flight and proceed as far as possible through the booking process. For an especially valuable redemption requiring a large points transfer, consider contacting the airline to confirm availability first.

Related: Phantom award space: What it is and how to avoid it

Many airline customer service agents are good at their jobs, but you’ll get much better results when you do the work yourself.

Before you call to book an award flight, you should have the exact dates and flight numbers you want. Make your specific requests known early in the conversation.

As soon as you tell the agent where you’re trying to go, say something like, “I have the flight numbers here whenever you’re ready for them.” This way, they don’t waste any time trying to search on their end.

If you’ve done your homework to ensure that there is award space and your routing is valid, these calls will go much more easily.

Ask the agent to confirm the complete itinerary, the number of points or miles required, and the applicable taxes and fees. Once booked, check that the reservation has been ticketed and that every flight is confirmed in the cabin you wanted.

Learning how to find and book award flights is one of the hardest things about award travel — especially when booking premium-cabin seats on a long flight.

Fortunately, tools like Seats.aero and Point.me make it much easier to compare loyalty programs and identify flights that might otherwise take hours to find. Both platforms offer free features, while paid subscriptions unlock more comprehensive searches and other useful tools that can be well worth the cost when hunting for a hard-to-find, long-haul premium-cabin award seat.

If you have a specific airline you wish to fly, use the tables above to search for award space and compare prices across programs before transferring any credit card points and booking your trip.

#6047. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”
